text:
Docker images, containers, registries and layers

Docker separates the application artifact from the running process. An image is a read-only template containing application files, runtime dependencies and metadata. A container is a runnable instance of an image with its own writable layer and process lifecycle. Images are normally pulled from or pushed to registries. A registry stores image content; a repository is a named collection of related images; a tag is a human-readable reference that can move over time. A digest identifies image content immutably.

For enterprise RAG, this distinction matters because the service should be reproducible: the same image digest should run the same code even when a mutable tag such as `latest` changes.

Dockerfile fundamentals

A Dockerfile describes how an image is built. Typical instructions include `FROM`, `WORKDIR`, `COPY`, `RUN`, `ENV`, `EXPOSE`, `USER` and `CMD`. `RUN` executes during image construction; `CMD` defines the default command when a container starts; `ENTRYPOINT` can make the container behave like a dedicated executable. Keep build-time dependencies out of the final runtime image when possible.

Layering and build cache

Docker builds are layered. Instructions that remain unchanged can reuse cached layers, while a change to an earlier step can invalidate later steps. Put stable dependency installation steps before frequently changing application source when this improves cache reuse. Do not treat the cache as a security boundary: build inputs, package sources and secret-handling must still be controlled.

Container lifecycle

Common lifecycle operations are `docker create`, `docker start`, `docker stop`, `docker restart`, `docker kill`, `docker rm` and `docker inspect`. `docker run` is a convenience that creates and starts a container. A stopped container preserves its writable layer until removed. A robust service should be stateless when possible and store durable state in an explicit volume or external service.

Environment variables and configuration

Environment variables are useful for non-secret configuration and for changing runtime behavior between environments. They should not be treated as a secure secret store. For credentials and keys, use a proper secret mechanism appropriate to the deployment environment. Avoid baking environment-specific secrets into images because images are portable artifacts and may be copied to other registries or systems.

Volumes and bind mounts

A named volume is managed by Docker and is suited to durable container data. A bind mount maps a host path into the container and is useful for development or when the host deliberately owns the files. Containers should not rely on their writable layer for database durability. For PostgreSQL, persistent storage should be designed independently of the application container lifecycle.

Docker networking basics

A container can connect to networks and communicate with other containers according to the network configuration. In Compose, services on the default project network can discover one another by service name. This is important for an enterprise stack: an API container can reach PostgreSQL using its Compose service name instead of relying on a hard-coded container IP address.

Port publishing

A container port does not automatically become reachable from the host. `-p HOST:CONTAINER` publishes a container port to the host. Binding to `127.0.0.1` can limit host exposure, while binding to `0.0.0.0` exposes the port on host interfaces. In production, avoid publishing internal database and metrics ports unless there is a clear requirement.

Health checks versus process state

A running container only proves that its main process has not exited. A health check can test whether the service is actually ready to serve requests. Health checks should be cheap, deterministic and representative of the service dependency contract. They should not accidentally trigger expensive model loading or database migrations repeatedly.

Reproducible image identity

For controlled deployments, prefer immutable image digests or pinned release versions over floating tags. Tags are convenient human references but can move. Reproducibility requires recording the exact application version, base image version, dependency lock state and, for high-assurance deployments, the final image digest.

Compose as a multi-service definition

Docker Compose lets a project describe multiple services, networks and volumes in one YAML model. An enterprise RAG stack can use Compose for local integration: FastAPI API, PostgreSQL metadata store, NGINX edge proxy, Prometheus metrics, and optional model/retrieval workers can be defined as separate services with explicit dependencies and health checks.

Service discovery in Compose

Compose creates a project network by default, and each service can be reached by its service name on that network. This avoids hard-coding container IP addresses. If a service is called `postgres`, an API container can generally use `postgres` as the database host. IP addresses can change when containers are recreated.

Dependency ordering and readiness

A dependency declaration can control startup order, but startup order is not the same as application readiness. A database process can be listening before initialization is complete. Prefer explicit health checks and application-side retry logic for dependencies that may take time to become ready.

Persistent PostgreSQL storage

A PostgreSQL container should use a persistent volume for its data directory. The application container should not share PostgreSQL's internal data files through a bind mount unless there is a deliberate reason and the host filesystem semantics are understood. Backups must be tested separately; a volume is not a backup.

Compose configuration separation

Keep environment-specific values in separate Compose override files or environment inputs. Avoid duplicating full service definitions across files. Separate safe defaults from secrets and document required variables. Never commit production credentials to the repository.

Internal versus external networks

Create separate networks when you want to reduce unnecessary connectivity. For example, an edge-facing NGINX service can be on an ingress network and an internal API/database network. Only the components that must communicate should join both. Network segmentation reduces accidental exposure and makes trust boundaries explicit.

Logging and troubleshooting Compose

Use `docker compose ps`, `docker compose logs`, `docker compose exec`, and `docker compose config` when debugging. `docker compose config` is particularly useful for checking the fully resolved configuration. When a request fails, trace the path: client -> NGINX -> API -> retrieval/model service -> PostgreSQL/vector store, and inspect logs at each boundary.

Resource limits and enterprise behavior

Local Compose is useful for reproducibility, but resource constraints should be made explicit when testing latency or memory. CPU, RAM and GPU availability can differ across environments. Never claim a latency result from a constrained development container is representative of production without recording the runtime environment.

Common networking failure modes

A service can fail because it uses `localhost` when it should use another service name, because the two containers are not attached to the same network, because the target port is confused with the published host port, or because an application is binding only to `127.0.0.1` inside the container. Debug from inside the calling container rather than assuming host-level connectivity is equivalent.

Compose and the RAG project

A good local stack keeps retrieval, reranking and generation components independently replaceable. That makes ablations easier: the same API and monitoring layer can call a generic retriever, a fine-tuned retriever, or the final trained pipeline while infrastructure remains constant.

Least privilege for containers

Run services as a non-root user when the service does not require root. Minimize installed packages and remove build-only tools from runtime images. Do not assume container isolation eliminates the need for operating-system permissions, filesystem restrictions or network controls.

Secrets in Docker builds

Build arguments and image layers should not be used as a convenient place to hide secrets. A value written into an image layer can survive even after the source line is removed. Use build secrets where supported for build-time credentials and inject runtime secrets through the deployment platform.

Image provenance and scanning

An enterprise build should record the base image, package set and application version. Image vulnerability scanning is useful but does not prove an application is secure. It complements code review, dependency pinning, minimal images, runtime hardening and network restrictions.

Troubleshooting HTTP 502 from a containerized API

A 502 at NGINX often means the proxy could not obtain a valid upstream response. Check that the API process is listening on the expected interface and container port, verify NGINX upstream configuration, test the upstream from inside the NGINX container, and inspect API logs. Do not fix a 502 by blindly increasing proxy timeouts before understanding whether the backend is reachable.

Troubleshooting slow model containers

Separate model-load time from request-time latency. Record startup duration, first-request latency, warm-request p50/p95 latency and resource usage. Model initialization may be dominated by weight loading, tokenizer setup or CPU memory pressure and should not be confused with retrieval or generation latency.

Container exit diagnosis

Start with `docker ps -a` and inspect the exited container. Check logs, exit code, configuration and mounted paths. Common causes include missing environment variables, wrong executable paths, permission errors, incompatible architecture, failed database connections and application exceptions.

RAG security boundary in containers

Do not give a retrieved document the ability to alter container commands or system configuration. Retrieved text is data, not authority. Keep model prompts, tool permissions, filesystem permissions and deployment credentials separate from knowledge-base content. This directly supports the project requirement to resist instruction-bearing and poisoned documents.

Auditability

Record image identifiers, deployment manifests, configuration versions and significant security changes. When a hidden benchmark exposes an attack, the team should be able to identify which container image and configuration produced the result.

Operational anti-patterns

Avoid running databases with random ephemeral storage, exposing every internal port, copying production secrets into local `.env` files, using `latest` for formal experiments, or changing an image manually inside a running container. Each practice makes reproducibility and incident investigation harder.

Corpus ingestion worker isolation

If corpus ingestion executes document parsing, conversion or code extraction, isolate that workload from the serving API. Untrusted documents can contain malicious payloads, enormous files or parser edge cases. A separate worker process or container with restricted permissions is safer than parsing arbitrary files inside the public API process.

FastAPI application object

A FastAPI application is created from the `FastAPI` class. Route handlers are declared with decorators such as `@app.get()` and `@app.post()`. FastAPI uses Python type annotations and Pydantic models to validate and document API input and output. The framework exposes an OpenAPI schema and interactive documentation for the API.

Path operations and HTTP methods

A path operation combines a URL path with an HTTP method. Common REST-style mappings use GET for retrieval, POST for creation or processing, PUT for replacement, PATCH for partial updates and DELETE for deletion. The project should choose semantics consistently and document exceptions when an endpoint represents an action such as `/evaluate` or `/search`.

Request path, query and body parameters

Path parameters are part of the route, query parameters are supplied in the URL query string, and request bodies carry structured payloads. Use Pydantic models for JSON request bodies when structure and validation matter. Keep path and query parameters narrow enough that API behavior is predictable.

Response models

Response models provide a contract for output. They can validate returned data and make OpenAPI documentation useful to consumers. In a RAG service, explicit response models can separate the answer text, citations, retrieval metadata, refusal state and evaluation fields instead of returning an unstructured dictionary.

Automatic OpenAPI documentation

FastAPI automatically generates an OpenAPI specification and interactive documentation. The documentation can be used by developers to understand endpoints and by automated tools to inspect the contract. This is an engineering advantage because API behavior and schema stay close to code.

Async versus normal path functions

FastAPI supports both `async def` and normal `def` path functions. Asynchronous functions are useful when the work is I/O-bound and the libraries involved support asynchronous use. CPU-heavy model inference does not become faster simply because the endpoint is declared `async`; CPU-bound work may need a worker process, queue or other execution strategy.

Status codes and error responses

Use meaningful HTTP status codes. Validation errors should be distinguishable from authentication failures, missing resources, dependency failures and internal server errors. Do not expose stack traces or sensitive infrastructure details to external clients.

Application lifecycle

Initialization can include loading configuration, opening shared clients, preparing telemetry and constructing service objects. Expensive model loading should happen once per worker process where appropriate rather than on every request. Be explicit about whether state is local to one process or shared through an external service.

API versioning

For an evolving enterprise service, version the public contract deliberately, for example through a URL prefix or another stable compatibility strategy. Do not silently change the shape of the answer or citation objects while evaluation and clients depend on the existing schema.

Request correlation

Attach a request identifier or correlation identifier to logs and response metadata when appropriate. The same identifier should help connect an NGINX access log, FastAPI request log, retrieval trace and Prometheus metrics without storing sensitive user content.

Dependency injection in FastAPI

FastAPI's dependency injection system lets a path operation declare required components such as a database session, authenticated user, configuration object or authorization rule. Dependencies can depend on other dependencies. This makes shared security and resource logic reusable without manually calling it in every endpoint.

Authentication and authorization

Authentication answers who the caller is; authorization answers what that caller is allowed to do. Use a standard authentication mechanism and explicit authorization checks. A caller authorized to query the RAG system may not automatically be authorized to upload or delete corpus documents.

OAuth2-oriented API flows

FastAPI provides helpers and interactive documentation for OAuth2-related flows. The exact flow should match the organization’s identity provider and security model. Store tokens securely, validate them server-side and keep authorization scopes narrow.

Dependency-driven database sessions

A database session dependency can create or acquire a connection for a request and ensure it is cleaned up. The service should not create a new heavyweight PostgreSQL client on every small helper call. Connection pooling should be configured according to concurrency and database capacity.

BackgroundTasks and long work

FastAPI can schedule background tasks that run after a response is returned. This is useful for small tasks where the client does not need to wait. It is not a replacement for a durable task queue for long-running corpus ingestion, multi-minute model training, GPU jobs or work that must survive process restarts.

File upload security

Corpus ingestion endpoints should restrict file size, allowed types, upload path and parsing behavior. Uploaded files should not be treated as executable code. Consider content-type validation, decompression limits and isolated processing for formats with complex parsers.

Prompt injection at the API boundary

The API should treat user queries and retrieved documents as untrusted input. Tool selection, system instructions, credentials and deployment operations must not become controllable merely because an input document contains imperative language.

Rate limiting and abuse control

A RAG API can be abused through high query volume, huge input contexts or repeated expensive retrieval requests. Rate limiting, request size limits, timeouts and concurrency controls reduce resource exhaustion. These controls should be measured rather than chosen arbitrarily.

CORS and browser exposure

Cross-origin configuration should allow only required origins rather than using a permissive wildcard by default in an authenticated production application. CORS is a browser policy, not a replacement for server-side authorization.

Security logging

Log security events such as authentication failures, authorization denials and rejected oversized uploads, but do not log passwords, bearer tokens or entire private documents. Redact secrets and sensitive values before they reach centralized logging.

RAG query endpoint design

A useful production endpoint can accept a query and optional retrieval controls, then return an answer object containing the answer, citations, refusal status and possibly retrieval trace identifiers. Keep internal model prompts and raw tool outputs out of the public response unless the contract explicitly requires them.

Health and readiness endpoints

Separate liveness from readiness. A liveness endpoint answers whether the process is alive. A readiness check answers whether required dependencies are available enough to serve traffic. Do not make liveness depend on PostgreSQL if a temporary database outage would cause an otherwise healthy process to be restarted continuously.

Timeouts and cancellation

Set explicit timeouts for upstream calls. Retrieval, reranking and generation can have different latency expectations. A single unbounded request can consume worker capacity and cause cascading failures. When possible, propagate cancellation and stop work after the caller has disconnected.

Streaming responses

Streaming can improve perceived latency by returning generated tokens or incremental events before the full answer finishes. It also changes error handling: the server may have already sent part of a response when a downstream failure occurs. Citation completeness and refusal behavior should be defined explicitly for streamed responses.

Observability hooks

Expose metrics for request count, latency, error rate, retrieval latency, reranker latency, generation latency and dependency failures. Include low-cardinality labels such as route and outcome; avoid putting user queries into metric labels because high-cardinality data can overload the metrics system.

Graceful degradation

When a non-critical component fails, the API should have a deliberate policy. It may refuse the query, use a safe fallback retriever, or return a dependency-unavailable response. Silent fallback to an unvalidated model can invalidate the evaluation protocol.

Evaluation endpoint isolation

Formal evaluation should use a separate command or restricted endpoint so normal users cannot modify benchmark prompts, scores or system selection. The visible benchmark should be frozen before major tuning to prevent overfitting.

Reproducibility metadata

Record model version, retriever version, reranker version, corpus snapshot and configuration version with formal experiment results. Store these values in machine-readable metadata rather than relying on memory or notebook cells.

Deployment with NGINX

A common deployment places NGINX in front of FastAPI. NGINX can terminate TLS and proxy traffic to the API service. The FastAPI process should be bound to its internal interface and not be directly exposed to the public network unless there is a deliberate reason.

Deployment with Kubernetes

On Kubernetes, the API container should be managed by a Deployment, exposed internally through a Service, and configured with probes and resource requests/limits. Configuration that varies by environment should be separated from the image where possible.

Workflow file location and structure

GitHub Actions workflow files use YAML and are stored under `.github/workflows`. A workflow contains one or more jobs. Jobs contain steps, and steps either run shell commands or invoke actions. The workflow should be treated as code: review changes, validate syntax and keep environment assumptions explicit.

Events and triggers

The `on` key defines events that can start a workflow, such as pushes, pull requests, manual dispatches or scheduled events. Trigger scope matters: a workflow that runs on every branch and pull request can consume unnecessary resources, while a workflow that is too narrowly triggered may fail to validate important changes.

Jobs and runners

A job executes on a runner environment. Jobs are independent by default and can be connected with `needs`. Use job boundaries to isolate build, test, security scan and deployment stages. Record the runner type when comparing performance results because CPU, memory and preinstalled tools affect timings.

Steps and shell commands

Each job has a sequence of steps. A step can run a command or call an action. Keep shell commands explicit and fail fast where appropriate. Avoid constructing shell commands directly from untrusted pull-request content.

Matrix testing

A matrix can run a job across multiple operating systems, Python versions or dependency configurations. Matrix tests are useful for a technical corpus project because parsing, indexing and serving code may behave differently across supported runtime versions.

Artifacts

Workflow artifacts are files produced by a run and retained for later inspection or download according to repository settings. Evaluation jobs can upload JSON/CSV metrics, logs, benchmark summaries and packaged reports as artifacts.

Caching dependencies

Dependency caching can reduce repeated installation time, but caches are not a trustworthy secret store. Cache content is not signed or verified, so workflows must avoid storing credentials or accepting untrusted cache writes that could alter files executed later.

Reusable workflows

Reusable workflows allow an organization to centralize common CI or deployment logic. When reusing workflows from another repository, treat the referenced workflow as code with privileges and review its source, inputs and permissions.

Job permissions

Use the minimum GitHub token permissions needed by a job. A read-only test job generally should not receive write access to repository contents. Separate release or deployment permissions from routine pull-request validation when possible.

Concurrency control

Concurrency settings can cancel superseded runs or serialize deployment workflows. This prevents multiple commits from deploying simultaneously to the same environment and makes deployment state easier to reason about.

Pinning third-party actions

GitHub recommends pinning actions to a full-length commit SHA when immutable references are required. Tags are convenient but can move. Pinning reduces the risk that a later tag change silently executes different third-party code in a privileged workflow.

Secrets handling

Secrets should be stored using GitHub's secret mechanisms and referenced only where necessary. Do not echo secrets, place them in artifacts, or write them into dependency caches. Be especially careful when workflows process forked pull requests or other untrusted contributions.

Pull request trust boundary

Pull-request code can be attacker-controlled. A workflow that checks out untrusted code and exposes sensitive repository or deployment credentials can become a privilege-escalation path. Separate untrusted test execution from privileged deployment steps.

Environment protection

Production deployment environments can require approvals or other protection rules. Use these controls to prevent automated workflows from changing production infrastructure merely because a build passed.

Reproducible evaluation workflow

The evaluation workflow should check out a fixed commit, obtain a known corpus snapshot, run the same commands and output machine-readable results. Do not let benchmark questions be altered as part of the normal pull-request workflow.

Dependency lock and cache keys

Use lock files where the package ecosystem supports them and make cache keys reflect the relevant lockfile and runtime version. A cache hit should mean a compatible dependency state, not merely a matching operating system name.

Release evidence

For productionization, store the image digest, chart version, Git commit and test/evaluation summary together. This creates a trace from deployed behavior back to source code and benchmark results.

AI coding assistant logging

This project requires an AI-use log for significant generated code or design decisions. The CI pipeline can validate that an AI-use log exists for major changes without assuming that generated code is correct. Metrics and experiment conclusions must always come from actual runs.

Failure artifact retention

When a benchmark or deployment fails, upload enough evidence to reproduce the failure: test output, configuration summary, commit identifier and sanitized logs. Do not upload secrets, raw credentials or private benchmark questions.

Workflow anti-patterns

Avoid `curl | bash` installation patterns from unknown sources, unpinned third-party actions in privileged jobs, broad write permissions, secrets in repository files and untrusted pull-request code running with deployment credentials.

CI stages for the RAG project

A practical pipeline can validate formatting and static checks, run unit tests, run retrieval data integrity checks, build the container image, run integration tests and publish evaluation artifacts. Expensive fine-tuning jobs can be separated from normal CI and launched through an intentional training workflow.

Corpus validation in CI

Treat the corpus as versioned data. CI can validate required metadata fields, duplicate rates, empty documents, malformed records, invalid source URLs, unexpected licenses and chunk-size distributions. This prevents bad data from silently entering a benchmark or training run.

Benchmark leakage checks

Automated checks should ensure that benchmark questions or answers are not accidentally copied into training examples. Exact-match checks, normalized text comparisons and source provenance checks can catch obvious leakage. More sophisticated semantic leakage checks can be added later.

Training workflow separation

Model fine-tuning can require GPU resources and longer run times. Keep the training workflow separate from the main test pipeline and make it accept explicit dataset/model/configuration versions. This supports reproducibility and makes it possible to compare experiments fairly.

Evaluation artifact schema

Every formal evaluation should emit a machine-readable record with system variant, corpus version, benchmark version, metrics, runtime, hardware and configuration identifiers. Human-readable charts can be derived from this record.

Container image promotion

Build an image once and promote the same immutable artifact between environments instead of rebuilding differently for each environment. The image digest should be the identity used when recording experiments or deployments.

Deployment verification

After deployment, run smoke tests against health and representative API endpoints. Verify metrics are being scraped and logs are flowing before declaring the deployment successful.

Rollback strategy

A deployment pipeline should support rollback to a known working image or chart version. Rollback is safer when releases are immutable and configuration changes are versioned.

Hidden benchmark protection

The hidden benchmark must not be embedded in the repository or visible workflow artifacts. Production CI should validate the public benchmark; the private benchmark remains mentor-controlled until the final evaluation.

One-command reproduction

The repository should expose a documented command that creates a clean environment, validates the selected corpus, runs evaluation and emits JSON/CSV results. GitHub Actions should call the same scripts rather than duplicating experiment logic in YAML.

Helm and Kubernetes

Helm is a package manager and templating tool for Kubernetes applications. A chart is a collection of files that describes a related set of Kubernetes resources. A release is an installed instance of a chart with a particular configuration.

Chart directory structure

A chart commonly contains `Chart.yaml`, `values.yaml`, a `templates/` directory and optional dependency or documentation files. `Chart.yaml` describes chart metadata and can declare dependencies. The `templates/` directory contains manifests that Helm renders into Kubernetes resources.

Chart.yaml versus values.yaml

`Chart.yaml` describes the chart itself: name, chart version, compatibility metadata and dependencies. `values.yaml` provides default configuration values for the templates. Users can override values during installation or upgrade.

Values precedence

Helm merges values from several sources. Chart defaults can be overridden by supplied values files and by command-line parameters such as `--set`; later or more specific inputs take precedence. This is useful for environment-specific settings but can also hide configuration if overused.

Template rendering

Helm templates are processed before Kubernetes receives the resulting manifests. Functions and conditional logic can choose which resources to emit. `helm template` renders locally and is useful for inspecting the generated YAML before installing it.

Named templates and helpers

Reusable template snippets should live in helper templates rather than being copied into every resource. This reduces duplication and makes naming conventions consistent across Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps and other resources.

Labels and annotations

Labels should be stable and semantically useful for selection, ownership and operations. Annotations hold non-selector metadata. Helm charts should use predictable labels for application name, instance, chart and managed-by information while allowing application-specific labels where appropriate.

Chart dependencies

A chart can declare other charts as dependencies. Dependencies should be versioned and reviewed like any other software dependency because they can change the resources and permissions installed in a cluster.

Secrets and values

Do not assume that putting a secret into `values.yaml` makes it secret. Helm values are configuration data and can appear in release metadata or CI logs depending on how they are supplied. Prefer external secret management when the platform provides it.

Compatibility metadata

Use chart metadata and Kubernetes version constraints where necessary to prevent installing a chart into an unsupported environment. Test the rendered manifests against the target cluster versions.

Helm install

`helm install` creates a release from a chart and values. Use explicit release names and namespaces in automation. For production, validate the rendered manifests and values before installation.

Helm upgrade

`helm upgrade` changes an existing release to a new chart/configuration state. Values can be supplied with `-f/--values` or `--set` and related options. The order of multiple values files matters because later files can override earlier ones.

Rollback mindset

A rollback returns a release to a previous known revision. Rollbacks are safest when application images, configuration and schema changes are compatible with the older release. A database migration that cannot be reversed can make an otherwise successful Helm rollback unsafe.

Atomic deployment behavior

Helm supports options that make an upgrade/install wait for resources and roll back on failure. This is useful when the team wants the release to return to a previous state instead of remaining partially upgraded, but it does not make external side effects transactional.

Dry-run and validation

Use `helm template`, `helm install --dry-run` or equivalent validation paths to inspect generated manifests and catch obvious errors before changing the cluster. Local template rendering does not perform every server-side API validation, so cluster-level validation is still important.

Release history

Helm keeps release revisions that can be inspected and used for rollback. Treat release history as operational evidence: record which chart version and values produced a given production state.

Hooks

Helm hooks can run jobs at lifecycle points such as pre-install or post-upgrade. Hooks are powerful but easy to misuse. A hook that changes external state can make a rollback incomplete, and hook resources may require explicit cleanup or policies.

Upgrade failure diagnosis

When an upgrade fails, inspect Helm status/history and the Kubernetes resources that were changed. A failing readiness probe may be caused by application startup, configuration, image pull issues, permissions or an upstream dependency rather than Helm itself.

Chart testing

A chart should be tested with representative values files, rendered manifest validation and deployment smoke tests. Maintain at least one minimal configuration and one production-like configuration to catch assumptions that only appear with optional features enabled.

Release reproducibility

Store the exact chart version, Git commit, values files and image digest used for a formal deployment. This makes it possible to reproduce or audit a release months later.

RBAC least privilege in charts

A chart should create only the Kubernetes permissions it needs. Avoid cluster-wide RBAC permissions when namespace-scoped access is enough. Review service accounts, Roles, ClusterRoles and bindings as part of chart security.

Pod security defaults

Charts should avoid privileged containers, host networking and unnecessary hostPath mounts. Run as a non-root user where supported, drop unnecessary Linux capabilities and use read-only filesystems when compatible with the workload.

Resource requests and limits

Define resource requests so the scheduler can place workloads predictably. Limits can protect a cluster from runaway resource usage, but setting arbitrary low limits can cause legitimate workloads to fail. RAG model services need realistic memory and CPU/GPU budgets derived from actual measurement.

Probes

Readiness probes control whether a pod should receive traffic; liveness probes detect a process that needs restart; startup probes can protect slow-starting applications from premature liveness failures. Probe endpoints should reflect actual application state.

Network policies

Where network policies are supported, restrict which pods can communicate. For example, only the API may need access to PostgreSQL, while an ingress controller should not need direct database access. Policy design should follow the service graph rather than broad allow-all rules.

Ingress and TLS boundaries

A chart can expose the API through an Ingress or gateway layer. TLS termination location should be explicit, and secrets containing certificates must be handled securely. Internal service traffic should not be assumed to be protected merely because edge traffic uses HTTPS.

ConfigMap versus Secret

Non-sensitive configuration belongs in ConfigMaps; confidential values belong in Secrets or an external secret store. Treat Kubernetes Secrets as sensitive data but do not confuse base64 encoding with encryption by itself.

Supply-chain controls

Pin image versions or digests, review chart dependencies and use trusted registries. The chart itself is executable configuration: a malicious template can create powerful resources. Review third-party charts before installing them into an enterprise cluster.

Pod disruption and availability

Production services may need disruption budgets and multiple replicas to tolerate planned maintenance. Availability mechanisms only help when the underlying application is stateless enough to support multiple instances.

Helm in CI/CD

CI should lint and render charts, validate manifests, and deploy a specific chart version with explicit values. Production credentials should be available only to the deployment stage that requires them.

Kubernetes control model

Kubernetes is a declarative platform for managing containerized workloads and services. Users describe a desired state, and controllers work continuously to reconcile the cluster toward that state. This differs from a script that simply starts processes once.

Pod

A Pod is the smallest deployable compute object in Kubernetes and represents one or more containers that share networking and selected storage namespaces. Containers in the same Pod communicate over `localhost`. Pods are generally replaceable rather than treated as permanent machines.

Deployment

A Deployment manages a set of replicated Pods and supports controlled updates. It specifies the desired number of replicas and the Pod template. Controllers create or replace Pods until the observed state matches the desired state.

Service

A Service provides a stable network abstraction for accessing a set of Pods selected by labels. Pods can change IP addresses as they are recreated, while the Service provides a stable endpoint for clients inside the cluster.

ConfigMap

ConfigMaps store non-sensitive configuration data. They can be exposed as environment variables or mounted as files. Changing a ConfigMap does not automatically mean an application reloads the new values; the application and deployment strategy must define how configuration changes take effect.

Secret

Secrets are intended for sensitive configuration such as credentials or tokens. They are not a substitute for an external secret management system, and base64 encoding is not equivalent to encryption. Access to Secrets should be restricted with RBAC.

Namespace

Namespaces partition names and can support policy and access-control boundaries. They are useful for separating environments or teams, but a namespace alone is not a complete security boundary.

Labels and selectors

Labels are key-value metadata used to identify and group resources. Selectors connect controllers and Services to the Pods they manage. A label mismatch can cause a Service to have no endpoints or a Deployment to fail to manage the intended Pods.

Jobs and CronJobs

Jobs run work to completion; CronJobs create Jobs on a schedule. They are suitable for one-off or periodic tasks such as re-indexing, backup verification or offline evaluation. Long-running API servers generally belong in Deployments instead.

Persistent volumes

Persistent storage separates application lifecycle from data lifecycle. PersistentVolumeClaims express storage requirements and can be bound to storage provided by the cluster. Stateful services require careful storage, backup and failover design; a Pod restart does not restore lost data by itself.

Kubernetes network model

Kubernetes gives Pods cluster-wide IP addresses and supports Pod-to-Pod communication through the cluster network, subject to network policies or other controls. Containers in a Pod share the Pod network namespace and can communicate through `localhost`.

Service discovery

Services are discoverable through cluster DNS. Applications should usually call the Service name rather than storing Pod IPs. This is fundamental for reliable communication between a FastAPI API and internal retrieval services.

Service types

ClusterIP exposes a Service inside the cluster. NodePort and LoadBalancer provide other exposure models depending on the environment. Ingress or gateway layers can provide HTTP routing and TLS termination for multiple services.

Ingress routing

An Ingress defines HTTP(S) routing rules for external access through an Ingress controller. The controller is the component that actually implements the routing. Do not assume that creating an Ingress object by itself creates a load balancer.

Readiness, liveness and startup probes

Readiness indicates whether a Pod should receive traffic. Liveness indicates whether a container should be restarted. Startup probes can protect slow-starting applications from liveness checks that would otherwise restart them during initialization.

Resource requests and limits

Requests influence scheduling and communicate the expected resource reservation. Limits constrain usage according to the resource type. Poorly chosen values can either waste capacity or cause throttling/OOM failures. Model services should be tested under realistic memory pressure.

Horizontal scaling

A Deployment can run multiple replicas. Horizontal Pod Autoscaling can adjust replica counts based on metrics. CPU utilization is not always a useful signal for a RAG service; request rate, queue depth or latency may better represent demand if custom metrics are available.

Scheduling constraints

Node selectors, affinity and taints/tolerations can influence where Pods run. GPU workloads often require node labels, resource requests and device-plugin support. Scheduling rules should be justified by workload requirements rather than copied blindly.

Graceful termination

When a Pod is terminated, applications should close connections and finish safe in-flight work before the termination deadline. HTTP servers should stop accepting new work while allowing current requests to finish within a bounded time.

Failure debugging path

For a failing Service, check `kubectl get`, `kubectl describe`, endpoints, Pod status, events and logs. Start from the client request and trace through Service selection, Pod readiness, container port binding and application logs.

RBAC

Kubernetes RBAC controls which identities can perform which actions on which resources. Prefer namespace-scoped Roles and RoleBindings when cluster-wide permissions are not required. Service accounts used by workloads should have only the permissions the application needs.

NetworkPolicy

Network policies can restrict traffic between Pods and from external sources. Start with a documented application communication graph, then allow only required flows. Policy behavior depends on a network plugin that supports the relevant features.

Pod security

Avoid privileged containers and unnecessary host access. Use security contexts to run as non-root, drop unnecessary capabilities and control filesystem mutability. Validate that the chosen constraints are compatible with the application runtime.

Resource isolation for model serving

Large models can consume substantial RAM or GPU memory. Set explicit requests and limits where appropriate and consider dedicated nodes or scheduling constraints. Record hardware details for performance experiments so p50/p95 latency comparisons are meaningful.

Secrets rotation

Secrets should be rotated when credentials expire or are suspected to be compromised. Applications need a defined reload strategy; mounting a new Secret does not guarantee that a process automatically starts using the new value if it copied the secret into memory at startup.

Audit and events

Kubernetes events and audit logs can help explain unexpected changes. For formal experiments, record the cluster version, chart version, image digests, namespace configuration and relevant events. Avoid relying solely on screenshots as evidence.

Backup and restore boundaries

Backing up manifests is not enough for stateful applications. PostgreSQL data, persistent volumes and application configuration have different recovery requirements. Define recovery objectives and test restoration.

Rolling updates

A rolling update replaces old Pods with new Pods while maintaining availability according to the Deployment strategy. Readiness probes are critical because a Pod should not receive traffic until it is actually ready.

Zero-downtime caveats

Zero downtime is not guaranteed by a rolling strategy alone. Schema migrations, singleton resources, slow startup, connection pools and downstream capacity can still create outages. Test the entire request path during rollout.

Kubernetes and the RAG capstone

The final capstone can run the API, retrieval services, reranker, generator and observability stack as separate workloads. This separation supports component ablations and resource measurement while preserving one consistent external interface.

Filesystem navigation

Core commands such as `pwd`, `ls`, `cd`, `find`, `stat`, `du` and `df` provide the basic vocabulary for investigating Linux systems. `df` describes filesystem capacity; `du` describes space consumed by files/directories. A full filesystem and a large directory are related but not identical diagnoses.

File permissions

Linux permissions distinguish read, write and execute for owner, group and other users. For regular files, execute permits running the file as a program; for directories, read permits listing entries, write permits creating/removing entries, and execute permits accessing entries. Permissions should be interpreted in the context of ownership and the directory path.

chmod and symbolic permissions

`chmod` changes permission bits. Symbolic forms such as `chmod u+x script.sh` express the intended change clearly. Numeric forms such as `chmod 640 file` set owner/group/other permission bits directly. Avoid `chmod -R 777` as a generic fix because it removes meaningful access control.

Ownership and groups

`chown` changes file ownership and `chgrp` changes group ownership. Group-based permissions are useful for shared application directories. Service users should receive access through explicit group membership or ACLs rather than broad world-write permissions.

Processes and signals

`ps`, `top`, `pgrep` and `pstree` help inspect processes. `kill` sends signals; `SIGTERM` requests graceful shutdown, while `SIGKILL` forces termination when a process cannot or will not exit. Prefer graceful signals for services so they can close files and connections.

Environment and PATH

`env`, `printenv`, `export` and `echo $PATH` help inspect environment variables. Environment configuration can change how software resolves commands and libraries. For reproducibility, record relevant environment variables but do not leak secrets into logs or experiment metadata.

Redirection and pipelines

Shell pipelines connect the standard output of one command to the standard input of another. `>`, `>>`, `<` and `2>` control redirection. A pipeline can hide errors when only the last command's status is checked; scripts should use appropriate shell error-handling options and explicit checks.

grep, sed and awk

`grep` searches text; `sed` performs stream editing; `awk` is useful for field-oriented processing. These tools are valuable for logs and configuration inspection, but avoid complex one-liners in production runbooks when a clearer script is safer.

archives and compression

`tar` packages files and can combine with compression tools such as gzip or zstd depending on the environment. Preserve file ownership and permissions when creating backups that are intended for system restoration, and validate the archive before trusting it.

system information

`uname`, `lscpu`, `free`, `lsblk`, `ip`, `ss` and related commands expose CPU, memory, storage and network state. Performance experiments should capture hardware/runtime information so model and retrieval latency can be interpreted correctly.

IP and route inspection

`ip addr` shows interfaces and addresses; `ip route` shows routing information. When a service cannot reach a dependency, check DNS, route, interface state and listening ports before assuming the application is broken.

Listening sockets

`ss -lntup` is a common way to inspect listening TCP/UDP sockets and associated processes where permitted. Confirm the address and port the process binds to. A process listening on `127.0.0.1` is not reachable through the host's external interface.

DNS troubleshooting

`getent hosts`, `resolvectl` where available, and tools such as `dig` or `nslookup` can help diagnose name resolution. DNS problems often appear as application connection timeouts, so distinguish name-resolution errors from TCP connection errors.

curl as an HTTP diagnostic

`curl -v` can show DNS resolution, TCP/TLS connection steps, request headers and response headers. It is useful for testing NGINX, FastAPI health endpoints and internal Services. Avoid sending credentials or tokens in command history on shared systems.

systemd services

`systemctl status`, `systemctl start`, `systemctl stop`, `systemctl restart` and `systemctl enable` manage systemd services. A service unit describes how a process is launched and supervised. After changing a unit file, reload the systemd manager configuration as appropriate before restarting the service.

journalctl

`journalctl` reads systemd journal entries. Use time, unit and priority filters to narrow the investigation. Logs are evidence of what the service reported, not proof that the reported root cause is correct; correlate with metrics and dependency logs.

CPU and memory pressure

Use `uptime`, `top`, `vmstat` and `free` to inspect system pressure. High load average can reflect CPU saturation, blocked I/O or runnable tasks, so it should not be interpreted as CPU percentage by itself.

Disk pressure

Use `df -h` to check filesystem capacity and `du -xh` to locate large directories. Also consider inode exhaustion. Containers, logs and model files can consume disk even when the application database itself appears healthy.

Log rotation

Unbounded logs can fill disks. Configure a retention policy and rotation mechanism appropriate to the operating system/container environment. Centralized logging is preferable for multi-node systems, but the local node must still prevent runaway storage use.

Resource limits and isolation

Linux namespaces and control groups underpin important forms of process isolation and resource control used by container platforms. Understanding these primitives helps explain why CPU, memory, filesystem and network behavior in containers differs from a simple process on the host.

API unreachable playbook

Check DNS, route, listening socket, local firewall, reverse proxy upstream and application logs in that order. A clear chain avoids changing multiple components simultaneously and losing the evidence about which boundary failed.

Database connection playbook

Confirm hostname resolution, port reachability, PostgreSQL listener configuration, authentication and database existence. Then check connection pool limits and PostgreSQL logs. Do not increase connection counts until the database capacity and workload are understood.

High memory playbook

Identify which process or container owns the memory, determine whether usage is steady or growing, and check for caches, model weights, large query results or leaks. For a RAG service, separate model memory, vector index memory and request concurrency effects.

High CPU playbook

Measure the process consuming CPU and correlate it with workload. CPU spikes may come from indexing, embedding generation, reranking, TLS, compression or pathological queries. Avoid treating a high CPU graph as a root cause by itself.

TLS failure playbook

Validate certificate chain, hostname, expiration, protocol versions and private-key permissions. Use `openssl s_client` and `curl -vk` carefully for diagnosis, but do not disable certificate validation as a permanent fix.

Permissions failure playbook

Inspect the effective user, groups, path permissions and mount ownership. Use `namei -l` to inspect each directory component and `stat` for file metadata. Prefer fixing the correct owner/group/ACL instead of granting world-write access.

Process leak playbook

Compare process counts over time, inspect child processes and open files, and correlate with request volume. A leak may be file descriptors, threads, subprocesses or memory rather than the number of top-level processes alone.

Incident evidence checklist

For reproducible incidents, collect UTC timestamps, host/container identifiers, deployment version, configuration hash, relevant logs, resource metrics and exact commands run. Avoid collecting secrets or unnecessary personal data.

Production change discipline

Make one meaningful change at a time during diagnosis, record the hypothesis, observe the effect and revert if it does not help. Ad hoc changes destroy the causal trail required for engineering learning.

Linux relevance to the capstone

The capstone ultimately runs on operating-system primitives whether through local services, containers or Kubernetes nodes. Understanding processes, sockets, permissions, logs and resource pressure helps explain failures that a Python traceback alone cannot.

NGINX request processing

NGINX can act as a web server, reverse proxy and gateway. In reverse-proxy mode it receives a client request, selects an upstream server, forwards the request, receives the upstream response and returns it to the client. This makes NGINX a natural edge layer for a FastAPI enterprise service.

server and location blocks

NGINX configuration is organized into contexts such as `http`, `server` and `location`. A `server` block selects a virtual host based on properties such as the requested hostname and port. A `location` block applies routing and proxy behavior to matching request paths.

proxy_pass

`proxy_pass` defines where an upstream request is sent. Be precise about URI rewriting behavior because the placement of a trailing slash can change the resulting path forwarded to the backend. Test actual request paths rather than relying on memory.

Forwarded headers

Reverse proxies commonly forward information about the original request, such as host and client address, through headers. Backend frameworks must be configured carefully to trust these headers only from known proxies. Blindly trusting client-supplied forwarding headers can create security problems.

Buffering and timeouts

NGINX can buffer upstream responses and has configurable connect, send and read timeouts. Increasing timeouts may help with legitimately long operations, but it also holds connections longer and can reduce concurrency. Tune timeouts with measured workload data.

Static content and API traffic

NGINX can serve static content directly while proxying API requests to FastAPI. This can reduce application work and make caching behavior explicit. Dynamic RAG responses usually should not be cached like immutable JavaScript assets unless the cache key and freshness semantics are carefully defined.

Client body limits

The proxy can enforce request-size limits. This is useful for corpus upload APIs because a very large file can consume memory, disk or parser time. The limit should align with the backend's own validation and with expected operational requirements.

Request logging

Access logs provide a high-level record of client requests. Log route, status, latency and upstream timing where useful, but do not put full confidential prompts or authorization tokens into access logs.

HTTP protocol behavior

HTTP method, headers and status codes form a contract between client, proxy and application. When debugging, compare the request at both sides of the proxy so header or path rewriting does not create hidden differences.

502, 504 and 499-style failures

A 502 often indicates an invalid or failed upstream response; a timeout-related 504 usually means the proxy did not receive an upstream response in time. Client-aborted requests may appear differently depending on NGINX configuration. Correlate the status with upstream logs and timing fields before changing configuration.

TLS termination

NGINX can terminate HTTPS by presenting a server certificate and using the corresponding private key. The private key must be protected. Modern configurations should use current TLS versions and strong configuration rather than legacy protocols and ciphers.

TLS certificate chain

A certificate proves the server identity within a trust model, but clients also need the appropriate chain. Incorrect certificate chains often produce browser or API-client validation failures even when the leaf certificate itself looks valid.

HTTP load balancing

NGINX can distribute HTTP/HTTPS traffic across an upstream group. Round-robin is a common basic algorithm; additional algorithms and capabilities depend on the NGINX edition and configuration. Load balancing can improve resource utilization and fault tolerance when application instances are compatible with horizontal scaling.

Health checks

Open-source NGINX provides passive health-check behavior for upstream failures; NGINX Plus adds active health-check capabilities. Do not describe active health checks as an Open Source feature without qualification.

Connection reuse

Keepalive connections can reduce repeated connection setup and TLS handshake overhead. Proper connection reuse can improve latency and reduce CPU use, but connection pool sizes should reflect upstream limits.

Rate limiting

Request rate limiting can protect expensive endpoints from abuse. A RAG query endpoint may deserve different limits from lightweight health endpoints. Limits should be aligned with expected request cost and should return predictable errors to clients.

Caching

NGINX can cache content, but caching dynamic answers requires careful consideration of identity, authorization, freshness and data sensitivity. A knowledge-base change can make a previously correct cached answer stale.

Upstream failure isolation

When one backend is unhealthy, traffic should be steered according to the configured load-balancing and health behavior. Clients still need sensible retry policies because retries can amplify load during an outage.

NGINX in Kubernetes

In Kubernetes, NGINX may run as an Ingress controller or as a standalone reverse proxy service. The deployment model changes how certificates, Service discovery and configuration are managed. Keep the conceptual boundary clear: Kubernetes routes traffic to the NGINX workload; NGINX applies HTTP proxy rules.

Observability at the edge

Record request count, response status and upstream latency. Exporting these values to the monitoring system lets the team distinguish edge latency from application, retrieval and generation latency.

Header hygiene

Do not blindly pass all client headers to upstream services. Explicitly define security-sensitive forwarding behavior and strip headers that could conflict with trusted proxy semantics.

Method restrictions

Endpoints can restrict methods using NGINX rules or application logic. The application should remain the authoritative authorization layer, while NGINX can reduce obvious unwanted traffic at the edge.

Path-based isolation

Separate public paths from internal administration and metrics paths. Monitoring endpoints should not be exposed to the public internet without a clear need and appropriate access controls.

TLS private-key permissions

The private key file needs restrictive filesystem permissions while remaining readable by the NGINX master process as required. A certificate is public information; the private key is not.

Security headers

Response headers can reduce some browser-side risks, but they do not replace application security. Choose headers based on the client behavior you actually support, and test them rather than copying an arbitrary header bundle.

Upload filtering

For corpus ingestion behind NGINX, enforce body-size limits and coordinate them with FastAPI validation. Reject obviously invalid inputs early, while keeping deeper file validation and parser isolation in the application/worker layer.

Operational reloads

NGINX can validate configuration before reloading. Prefer a configuration-test step before deployment so a syntax error does not replace a known-good configuration with a broken one.

Zero-downtime reload expectations

A reload can apply new configuration without fully restarting the master process, but application-level availability still depends on upstream health and connection behavior. Test reloads under real traffic before treating them as universally zero-downtime.

Access-log privacy

Logs should contain enough information to debug but not enough sensitive data to become a secondary data breach. Do not log authorization headers, credentials or full private prompts.

NGINX role in RAG security

NGINX is an edge control, not the RAG security verifier. The final system still needs source trust policies, instruction-data separation, citation checking and fail-closed behavior inside the application pipeline.

Relational model

PostgreSQL stores data in tables with rows and typed columns. Primary keys identify rows; foreign keys describe relationships between tables. Normalize data where appropriate to reduce update anomalies, but use deliberate denormalization when measured read performance or analytics requirements justify it.

DDL and DML

DDL defines database structure, such as `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE` and `CREATE INDEX`. DML changes or retrieves data, including `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `SELECT`. Transaction boundaries determine when groups of changes become durable and visible according to the isolation rules.

Constraints

Constraints such as `PRIMARY KEY`, `UNIQUE`, `NOT NULL`, `CHECK` and `FOREIGN KEY` encode data integrity rules close to the database. Application validation remains useful, but database constraints protect the data even if another client bypasses the application.

Transactions

Transactions group operations into an atomic unit. `COMMIT` makes the transaction durable according to configured durability semantics, while `ROLLBACK` discards the transaction's uncommitted changes. Long transactions can hold resources and interfere with maintenance, so keep transactional scope appropriate.

MVCC

PostgreSQL uses multiversion concurrency control (MVCC). Statements read a snapshot of data according to transaction visibility rules, which reduces the need for read operations to block writes. MVCC behavior is central to understanding isolation, vacuuming and concurrent workloads.

Isolation levels

PostgreSQL supports transaction isolation levels that trade concurrency and anomaly prevention. The application should choose the weakest level that satisfies its correctness requirements instead of assuming the strictest level is always best.

Locks

PostgreSQL uses locks for operations that require coordination. Row and table locks can still matter even with MVCC. Unexpected blocking should be diagnosed with PostgreSQL lock and activity views rather than fixed by restarting the database blindly.

Roles and privileges

PostgreSQL roles control authentication and authorization. Grant only the privileges required for the application. Avoid running the application as a superuser. Separate migration permissions from routine query permissions when practical.

Parameterized SQL

Applications should parameterize user-controlled values rather than constructing SQL strings by concatenation. This prevents SQL injection and improves statement reuse. Database permissions provide a second line of defense.

Connection management

Each PostgreSQL connection consumes resources. Application pools should be sized according to PostgreSQL capacity, transaction duration and actual concurrency. Too many connections can increase memory and context-switching costs rather than increasing throughput.

Why indexes exist

An index can let PostgreSQL locate qualifying rows faster than scanning an entire table, but indexes add write and storage overhead. More indexes are not automatically better. Every index should have a workload reason.

B-tree indexes

B-tree is the general-purpose index type used for many equality, range and ordering queries. It is often the default starting point for ordinary scalar columns, subject to actual query patterns.

GIN, GiST and BRIN

PostgreSQL supports several index types with different data-structure strengths. GIN is useful for certain composite and containment-style workloads; GiST supports generalized search structures; BRIN summarizes physical ranges and can be very small for naturally ordered large tables. Choose based on operator and data characteristics.

Composite indexes

A multi-column index can support queries that constrain or order by multiple columns. Column order matters. Test real query plans because an index that seems logically appropriate may still be unused or dominated by another access path.

Partial indexes

A partial index covers only rows satisfying a predicate. This can make an index smaller and more selective when the application repeatedly queries a subset such as active records. The query predicate must be compatible enough for the planner to use the index.

Expression indexes

An index can be built on an expression, such as a normalized form of a value. This is useful when queries repeatedly apply the same transformation. The expression must match planner expectations and the workload should justify the extra write cost.

EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE

`EXPLAIN` shows the planned execution strategy. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually executes the query and reports observed timing and row counts. Because it executes the statement, use caution with writes and production data. Compare estimated versus actual cardinalities to diagnose planner misestimates.

Statistics and ANALYZE

The planner relies on table statistics to estimate row counts and choose plans. `ANALYZE` updates statistics. Stale or insufficient statistics can produce poor plans even when indexes exist.

Slow query diagnosis

Start with the actual query, parameters and execution plan. Identify scans, joins, sorts, I/O and row-estimate errors. Do not add an index before understanding whether the bottleneck is CPU, I/O, locking, network transfer or application misuse.

RAG metadata indexing

For the capstone, PostgreSQL can store document metadata, source identifiers, version tags, ingestion status, evaluation records and experiment metadata. Index fields used for filtering, but avoid placing large document bodies into indexes merely because they exist in the table.

PostgreSQL backup approaches

PostgreSQL documents three broad backup approaches: SQL dumps, filesystem-level backups and continuous archiving. Each has different recovery characteristics. The correct choice depends on database size, recovery objectives and operational constraints.

pg_dump

`pg_dump` produces a logical dump of a database. It is useful for migrations, selective restoration and version transitions, but it is not identical to a physical continuous backup. Test restoring the dump rather than assuming the dump file is sufficient evidence of recoverability.

Point-in-time recovery

Continuous archiving can combine a base backup with archived WAL to support point-in-time recovery. This is appropriate when recovery needs are stricter than a periodic logical dump can provide.

Backup validation

A backup process is incomplete until restoration has been tested. Validate that the restored database contains the expected schema, roles or post-restore setup, critical rows and application connectivity.

Autovacuum and table health

PostgreSQL's MVCC model creates obsolete row versions that require cleanup. Autovacuum helps maintain table health and statistics. Disabling it without a strong reason can cause table and transaction-ID problems.

Monitoring database health

Track connections, transaction age, locks, query latency, cache behavior and storage growth. PostgreSQL exposes statistics views for many of these signals. Pair database metrics with application request traces so slow API requests can be mapped to database behavior.

Security boundaries

Restrict database network access to trusted application components, use strong authentication, separate roles by purpose and rotate credentials. Database backups and dumps can contain sensitive information and must be protected accordingly.

Schema migration discipline

Schema changes should be versioned and applied through a controlled migration mechanism. Large table rewrites or long locks can cause outages. Design migrations to be compatible with the rolling application version when deployments are not atomic.

Connection pool and idle sessions

A large number of idle connections can exhaust database capacity. Monitor connection states and identify connection leaks. Prefer a bounded application pool or external pooler when the architecture needs one.

PostgreSQL in the enterprise RAG architecture

Use PostgreSQL for authoritative structured metadata and operational state, not as a substitute for the vector index unless the architecture deliberately chooses a PostgreSQL-based vector solution. Separate the concerns of relational metadata, retrieval index and object/document storage.

Prometheus data model

Prometheus stores data as time series: timestamped samples identified by a metric name and a set of label dimensions. A unique combination of metric name and label values identifies a series. This dimensional model makes filtering and aggregation central to PromQL.

Metric names

Metric names should describe the measured feature. Counters commonly use a `_total` suffix. Names should stay predictable and avoid encoding unbounded identifiers that belong in labels.

Labels and cardinality

Labels distinguish series such as HTTP method or service. Every unique label-value combination creates a distinct series. High-cardinality labels such as request IDs or raw user queries can create enormous numbers of series and should not be used casually.

Counter, gauge, histogram and summary concepts

Counters represent quantities that generally increase and can reset on restart. Gauges represent values that can rise or fall. Histograms sample observations into buckets and can be used to approximate distributions and quantiles. Summaries calculate quantiles client-side with different aggregation trade-offs.

PromQL selection

PromQL selects and transforms time series. Label matchers filter the series set, and functions/operators aggregate, transform or calculate rates. Learn the difference between an instant vector, range vector and scalar because many query errors are type-shape errors.

Rate and increase

`rate()` is commonly used with counters to calculate the per-second average increase over a range. `increase()` returns the total increase over the selected range. Use counter-aware functions rather than dividing raw counter values by time manually.

Aggregation

Functions such as `sum`, `avg`, `max`, `min` and `count` can aggregate series. `sum by (...)` keeps selected labels while reducing dimensions. Before aggregating, decide which labels preserve an operational question and which are accidental detail.

Recording rules

Recording rules precompute frequently used or expensive expressions and store the result as a new time series. They can make dashboards and alerts faster and reduce repeated query cost.

Time-series naming for RAG

Useful metrics for the capstone include request totals, request duration histograms, retrieval duration, reranker duration, generation duration, refusal totals and citation verification outcomes. Keep labels low-cardinality: service, route, outcome and model version can be reasonable dimensions if bounded.

Prometheus versus logs

Metrics answer numerical questions over time; logs hold detailed event context. A mature system uses both and connects them through timestamps and correlation identifiers without copying entire user content into metric labels.

Scrape model

Prometheus normally pulls metrics from configured targets at intervals. The configuration describes scrape jobs and targets and can also load rule files. A target can be an application endpoint or an exporter exposing metrics on behalf of another system.

Configuration reload

Prometheus can reload configuration without restarting when the relevant lifecycle mechanism is enabled and the new configuration is valid. Validate configuration before relying on an automated reload in production.

Exporters

Exporters convert metrics from systems that do not expose Prometheus metrics directly. An exporter should produce stable, useful metrics and avoid exposing secrets or unbounded dimensions.

Recording rules versus alerting rules

Recording rules save computed time series for later use. Alerting rules create alert state when a PromQL expression returns matching series. Both are defined in YAML rule files and evaluated periodically.

Alert `for` duration

An alert rule can use a `for` duration so a condition must remain true for a period before the alert becomes firing. This helps reduce noise from transient spikes, but it also delays notification.

Alert labels and annotations

Labels classify alerts for routing and grouping; annotations provide human-readable context. Avoid putting raw high-cardinality identifiers into alert labels unless the alerting system can safely handle them.

Common infrastructure alerts

Useful alerts include API error-rate increases, sustained high latency, database connection saturation, disk-space exhaustion, missing scrape targets and repeated Pod restarts. Each alert should have a meaningful response action, not merely a scary threshold.

Missing data versus zero

No sample is not automatically equivalent to a metric value of zero. Queries and alerts should distinguish a genuinely observed zero from a target that stopped exposing data. This is especially important for scrape failures.

Promtool validation

The `promtool` utility can validate rule files. Automated CI should reject malformed rules before deployment to avoid losing observability at runtime.

Alert fatigue control

Start with alerts tied to user impact or actionable resource exhaustion. Add low-level diagnostic alerts as annotations or dashboards rather than sending every metric anomaly to an on-call channel.

Request latency decomposition

Record separate latency measurements for edge proxy, API processing, retrieval, reranking, generation and database access. End-to-end latency alone does not reveal which component is responsible for regressions.

p50 and p95

The p50 represents the median experience, while p95 shows a slower tail. The capstone explicitly requires p50/p95 reporting, so both should be calculated from the same defined request population and time window.

Throughput and saturation

Track requests per second, active requests and queue depth where available. High throughput with rising latency can indicate saturation. The system should record hardware and concurrency settings for each formal experiment.

Resource metrics

CPU, RAM and GPU metrics help explain model-serving behavior. Record them alongside benchmark runs rather than assuming the same model has the same performance on every environment.

Citation verification metrics

Expose counters for SUPPORTED, PARTIAL and UNSUPPORTED claims. A useful dashboard can compare citation support rate with answer correctness and refusal behavior instead of treating one metric as sufficient.

Adversarial benchmark observability

Record attack-class outcomes such as instruction-bearing documents, contradictory documents and outdated documents. Do not expose private benchmark content in public dashboards. Track labels such as attack class and outcome, not the hidden question text itself.

Monitoring model versions

Include a bounded model or pipeline version label in metrics so a deployment can be compared with a previous version. Do not use a Git commit hash as an unbounded label if the system generates a new series for every commit over long periods.

SLO-style thinking

Define expected availability and latency targets only after measuring real workloads. A target should be paired with a service-level indicator and an explicit interpretation of what counts as an error or unavailable response.

Failure correlation

When a latency spike occurs, correlate Prometheus data with NGINX access logs, FastAPI logs, Kubernetes events and PostgreSQL activity. A single metric rarely proves root cause.

Evaluation dashboard

The project requires a dashboard comparing system variants. It should show retrieval metrics, answer metrics, security results, latency and resource usage, with a clear corpus/benchmark/version selector so results are not mixed across incompatible runs.

Reference request path

A representative enterprise path is client -> NGINX/TLS -> FastAPI -> query processing -> hybrid retrieval -> reranker -> context selection -> generator -> citation verifier -> response. PostgreSQL can store structured metadata and experiment state, while a vector index stores dense retrieval data. Prometheus monitors the runtime. Docker packages services; Kubernetes and Helm can deploy them; GitHub Actions can build, test and promote artifacts.

Trust boundaries

Treat client queries, uploaded documents, retrieved passages and external model outputs as untrusted data. Deployment credentials, tool permissions, system instructions and monitoring administration belong to a higher-trust control plane. The RAG security layer must prevent retrieved instructions from crossing that boundary.

Version axes

Formal evaluation requires separate versions for corpus snapshot, benchmark, chunking/index configuration, retriever, reranker, generator, prompt/configuration and serving image. Changing any one of these can change results.

Resource boundaries

The serving system should isolate expensive generation and indexing operations from lightweight API and proxy processes. Resource requests and limits should be based on measurements. Formal latency results should record hardware and concurrency.

Deployment boundaries

A container image is an immutable application artifact; Helm/Kubernetes define deployment state; NGINX exposes the HTTP edge; FastAPI defines the service contract; PostgreSQL holds structured state; Prometheus observes behavior. Clear boundaries make experiments and failures attributable.

Corpus-to-answer trace

A robust answer trace should identify which corpus snapshot was indexed, which retriever and reranker selected passages, which citations supported claims and which model generated the answer. This is more useful than logging a prompt alone because it makes provenance auditable.

Hidden-benchmark protection

The mentor-controlled hidden benchmark should not be baked into training artifacts, public CI outputs or production dashboards. Evaluation infrastructure should make it technically difficult to accidentally mix hidden questions with the development corpus.

Change approval
